content.summary_of_the_paper:
I have read the authors' response and other reviewers' comments, and thus remain the evaluation unchanged.
=====================
This paper proposes kernel SGD for efficient second-order optimization with theoretical guarantees, in which the Hessian matrix is substituted by kernel matrix, which benefits from computational and memory efficiency. The experimental results demonstrates the superiority of the proposed kernel SGD.
content.main_review:
Pros:
This paper is well-written. The proposed algorithm is simple and exact, benefiting from kernel methods. The optimization problem can be transformed to a new space via the Hessian matrix of kernel machines. The cross entroy loss can be guaranteed to be non-increasing when compared to the original optimization problem.

Cons:
I’m familiar with kernel methods but not an expert in optimization. I concern the following issues:
1, this algorithm is only suitable to kernel methods based (second-order) optimization? If the optimization problem is not related to kernel methods, the Hessian matrix is not the kernel matrix?

2, there are many efficient second-order optimization, e.g., Hessian matrix approximation based algorithms, BFGS’s variants. It would better to take them into discussion for theory and experiments.

3, it appears a little strange why L-BFGS only achieves 87.77% accuracy on MNIST. The result is too low.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper introduces kernel matrix in second-order optimization with theoretical guarantees and experimental validations.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2954 by Reviewer diqz
display_title: We thank you for your valuable review!

content.title: We thank you for your valuable review!
content.comment:
Thank you for your acceptance recommendation! Here are our responses to the concerns.

*C1: This algorithm is only suitable to kernel methods based (second-order) optimization? If the optimization problem is not related to kernel methods, the Hessian matrix is not the kernel matrix?*

R1: Our proposed Kernel SGD is designed for neural network training. The key insight is that the neural network and the kernel both can produce a new representation of the original instance. The application of Kernel SGD on neural network training is an example of applying it to the optimization problem which is not related to kernel methods, while the Hessian matrix can still be constructed based on the training instances.

*C2: There are many efficient second-order optimizations. It would be better to take them into the discussion for theory and experiments.*

R2: We have added the comparison experiments of ADAHESSIAN [1] and multi-batch L-BFGS [2]. The results are promising as shown in the table below on the two data sets tested (i.e., *mnist*,   *cifar10* ). As ADAHESSIAN and multi-batch L-BFGS are very slow, the tests on larger data sets are in progress, but they have no hope to outperform Kernel SGD. Moreover, Kernel SGD shows a better generalization performance than ADAHESSIAN and multi-batch L-BFGS. More importantly, the convergence of ADAHESSIAN is about 26 times slower than Kernel SGD on *cifar10*.

| data set | optimizer| train. accuracy (\%) | test accuracy (\%) | converg. time (sec.) |
| ------- | -------| --------- | -------- | ------------- |
| mnist   | ADAHESSIAN| 99.23     | 97.31    | 175.92        |
| mnist   | multi-batch L-BFGS| 100.00     | 95.64    | 143.70  
| cifar10 | ADAHESSIAN| 99.29     | 82.88    | 12469.07      |
| cifar10 |multi-batch L-BFGS|100.00| 77.17|7991.27|

*C3: It appears a little strange why L-BFGS only achieves 87.77\% accuracy on MNIST. The result is too low.*

R3: It results from the size of historical gradients in L-BFGS which was set to 3 in our experiments. The larger size of historical gradients generally produces better results. However larger size of historical gradients didn't fit in the memory and thus we used the size of 3. We have added this implementation detail in the last paragraph of Section 4.1.

References:   

[1] Zhewei Yao, Amir Gholami, Sheng Shen, Kurt Keutzer, and Michael W Mahoney. Ada-hessian: An adaptive second-order optimizer for machine learning.AAAI (Accepted),2021.

[2] Bollapragada, Raghu, et al. "A progressive batching L-BFGS method for machine learning." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2018.

replying_to: Replying to Efficient Second-Order Optimization for Deep Learning with Kernel Machines
display_title: Official Review of Paper2954 by Reviewer zCMe

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a stochastic gradient descent for kernel machines, that uses the Hessian to precondition the update. The Hessian is the same as the kernel matrix, hence can be computed quite fast. The paper presents experimental results on several small datasets showing that kernel SGD achieves accuracies similar to existing second order algorithms, but substantially faster.
content.main_review:
The main contribution of the paper is the Kernel SGD algorithm. The authors prove that the algorithm converges, and also show that the algorithm works in practice on small datasets.

My main concern with the paper is the presentation.
- Please include the pseudo-code for the algorithm.
- In all cases, please state the dimensions of the matrices.
- What is the kernel you use? In section 3.2, you say that the input to the last layer is the \phi(x), but then you also state that the Hessian, which is the same as the Kernel SGD matrix is constant throughout training. If K(x, y) = <\phi(x), \phi(y)>, and \phi(x) is changing as a result of training, how can the Hessian stay constant?
- You assert that the Hessian for equation (1) is the Kernel matrix. However this was not clear to me, even after I read the supplementary material. 
- Your convergence theorem is a non-increasing theorem - it does not show convergence as stated.
- The proposition on page 5 is a very vague qualitative statement - it needs to be precise.
- In the proof of the proposition, you say "When sqrt(n) || ... || < 1", do you have results that show that this is indeed the case?
- Minor point --- on page 5, you flip the sign of the last term in ai −aj −yi +yj.

Experiments:
Your experiments got a test accuracy of 97.86 on MNIST with Resnet-18 --- this is very surprising --- even a 4 layer network can get to 99% on this dataset. Similarly, Resnet-18 can easily get to 93% on Cifar10 (https://github.com/kuangliu/pytorch-cifar), yet your numbers are closer to 83. Thus these results are not convincing.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper was quite hard to follow, as the presentation was not very clear.
The experimental results were not convincing - the baselines used were very poor.

display_title: We thank you for your valuable review!

content.title: We thank you for your valuable review!
content.comment:
*C1: Please include the pseudo-code for the algorithm.*

R1: We have added the pseudo-code of Kernel SGD with discussion in Section 3.2.

*C2: In all cases, please state the dimensions of the matrices.*

R2: We have added the dimensions of all the matrices that are presented in this paper.

*C3: What is the kernel you use? In section 3.2, you say that the input to the last layer is the $\phi(x)$, but then you also state that the Hessian, which is the same as the Kernel SGD matrix is constant throughout training. If $K(x, y) = <\phi(x), \phi(y)>$, and $\phi(x)$ is changing as a result of training, how can the Hessian stay constant?*

R3: $\phi(x)$ is the mapping function in the kernel machine and can produce a new representation for the original instance. As $\phi(\cdot)$ is determined by the kernel function and $x$ is the training instance, $\phi(x)$ is a constant during training. Since the Hessian consists of a set of $<\phi(x), \phi(y)>$ which is a constant, the Hessian is therefore a set of constants and is unchanged in the training. Besides, $\phi(x)$ in the kernel machine is not equal to but can be regarded to be corresponding to the input of the last layer in a neural network.


*C4: It is not clear how the Hessian for equation (1) is the kernel matrix.*


R4:  Sorry for your confusion. We have reorganized Section 2 in the manuscript and Section 1 in the supplementary material. The first derivative of the objective with respect to $\alpha$ is shown as Equation 5 in the supplementary material. From Equation 5, the second order derivative with respect to an $\alpha$ is a kernel value and thus the Hessian matrix which is formed by all the second-order derivatives (i.e., kernel values) is then the kernel matrix. 


*C5: Your convergence theorem is a non-increasing theorem - it does not show convergence as stated.*

R5: We have improved the theorem. As the minimum value of the loss J(W) is 0 according to its definition (cf. 4 lines above Equation 6), the training process terminates either when no further progress can be made (i.e., stay unchanged for a number of iterations) or when the loss becomes 0. 

*C6: The proposition on page 5 is a very vague qualitative statement - it needs to be precise.*

R6: We have revised the Proposition in Section 3.3 to make it more precise.

*C7: In the proof of the proposition, you say ''When $sqrt(n) ||...|| < 1$'', do you have results that show that this is indeed the case?*

R7: We have improved the proposition and its proof. The condition holds when the sum of the eigenvalues of the Hessian equals to 1/$n_c$, where $n_c$ is the number of classes of the learning problem. 

*C8: Minor point: on page 5, you flip the sign of the last term in $a_i -a_j -y_i +y_j$.*

R8: We have fixed this typo in $a_i-a_j-y_i +y_j$ in the proof of Convergence Theorem.

*C9: Resnet-18 can easily get to 93\% on Cifar10 (https://github.com/kuangliu/pytorch-cifar), yet your numbers are closer to 83. These results are not convincing .*

R9: In our experiment, the accuracy achieved on *cifar10* is around 83\% because we did not use the *RandomCrop()* and *RandomHorizontalFlip()* functions for image data which were used in the examples on the Github (https://github.com/kuangliu/pytorch-cifar). These two functions are used to pre-process the images in *cifar10* which randomly crop and flip the images. Since we did not adopt pre-processing procedures on other types (i.e., tabular and text) of training data, we 
omitted these two functions on image data either for fair comparison. We further evaluate *cifar10* with these two functions using SGD and obtained 92.73\% accuracy which is similar to the 93\% accuracy shown on the Github. We have added this explanation in the second paragraph of Section 4.2.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2954 by Reviewer LNKd

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper explores second-order optimization for deep learning by leveraging kernel machines.
content.main_review:
1. Please correct me if I am wrong; but the use of the term “linearly separable” sounds incorrect to me here: “A kernel machine uses the kernel trick to map the non-linear problem into a feature space where the problem is linearly separable.” The data might still be linearly inseparable in the higher dimensional space.
2. The expression in Eq. (1) is the Lagrangian. Is the dual problem stated somewhere?
3. Assuming c in Eq. (1) denotes the labels; did you mean the loss \ell(f(X), c) is a convex function and not affine?
4. In Figure 1, the values of the contour lines are so close to each other that the difference could be due to numerical precision error or noise. Hence, I’m not sure if this is a fair statement: “Kernel SGD found a better solution than the existing methods.”
5. I think the argument that “In the transformed space of Kernel SGD, the optimum tends to be closer to the initial position, and hence Kernel SGD is more likely to converge to a better solution with a higher speed” is not thoroughly justified. In particular, I find that it is not fair to argue that it converges with a higher speed since the optimum being closer to the initial point does not imply any information about the convergence speed. Maybe a result on convergence rate is needed?
6. Is the regularization coefficient set to 10^{-4} for all the methods? If so, do authors have an argument why this parameter shouldn’t be tuned for every method separately? I believe this approach may lead to unfair empirical comparisons. 
7. There is a typo here: “Figure 2: Trianing loss of each optimization method”.
content.summary_of_the_review: In my opinion, some of the “main” claims made in the paper require further justification/proof. Hence, my evaluation for the paper is negative.

content.comment:
*C1: ''A kernel machine uses the kernel trick to map the non-linear problem into a feature space where the problem is linearly separable.''-The use of the term ``linearly separable'' sounds incorrect.*

R1: We've corrected it. It should be ''may be linearly separable''.

*C2: The expression in Eq. (1) is the Lagrangian. Is the dual problem stated somewhere ?*

R2: We've reorganized Section 2, and now Eq. (1) is in primal form.

*C3: Assuming c in Eq. (1) denotes the labels; did you mean the loss $\ell(f(X), c)$ is a convex function and not affine?*

R3: The loss is assumed to be a convex and affine function. We've reorganized the equations in Section 2 for clarity. 

*C4: In Figure 1, the values of the contour lines are so close to each other that the difference could be due to numerical precision error or noise. Hence, I’m not sure if this is a fair statement: ''Kernel SGD found a better solution than the existing methods.''*

R4: The closed values of the contour lines are not resulted from numerical precision error or noise. For ease of visualization, we only updated two random weights of the neural network in each training iteration, the loss was updated with the two weights correspondingly. Thus, the small changes of two weights lead to the small changes of loss. 

*C5:The proposition is not thoroughly justified. It is not fair to argue that it converges with a higher speed since the optimum being closer to the initial point does not imply any information about the convergence speed. Maybe a result on convergence rate is needed?*

R5: We've revised the proposition and remove the ''higher speed'' in the proposition. The convergence rate of our Kernel SGD is the same as SGD in solving convex problems which is $O(1/t)$ with a constant learning rate and $t$ denotes the number of iterations. The derivation is similar as in [3] except that we put an inverted positive semi-definite matrix behind the gradient. 


*C6: Is the regularization coefficient set to $10^{-4}$ for all the methods? If so, do authors have an argument why this parameter shouldn't be tuned for every method separately? I believe this approach may lead to unfair empirical comparisons.*

R6: The regularization coefficient was set to $10^{-4}$ for all the methods following the setting in the popular studies [1,2]. The same coefficient for all the methods leads to a fair comparison, because different regularization coefficients lead to different objectives, which makes different methods incomparable. We have added this explanation in the last paragraph of Section 4.1.


*C7: There is a typo here: “Figure 2: Training loss of each optimization method”*

R7: Thank you for pointing out. We have fixed this typo in the caption of Figure 2.

[1] Kaiming He, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren, and Jian Sun. Deep residual learning forimage recognition. InProceedings of the IEEE conference on computer vision andpattern recognition (CVPR), pp. 770–778, 2016.

replying_to: Replying to Efficient Second-Order Optimization for Deep Learning with Kernel Machines
display_title: Official Review of Paper2954 by Reviewer bNM5

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a projection step on the gradient of final, fully connected layers to incorporate second-order information during SGD.  The projection chosen is a kernel matrix.  Under this setting, convergence guarantees and rates are provided.  Experimental results are provided evaluating the proposed method on several datasets and comparing to second-order solvers L-BFGS and ESGD, as well as vanilla SGD and SGD with momentum.
content.main_review:
The projection idea and theoretical results are interesting.  However, the paper contains problems with benchmark comparisons, unjustified design choices, and a potentially misleading description of the proposed method.

With regards to benchmark comparisons, several relevant works are not compared to (or even mentioned).  In particular, while the paper claims:
 ".., updating the Hessian matrix while training the networks is practically infeasible in most second-order optimization,"
there has been significant progress in recent years to develop second-order optimizers for SGD in deep learning, most notably [1, 2].  Furthermore, the comparison to L-BFGS, as implemented in PyTorch, presented in the paper is extremely questionable; this version of L-BFGS operates in full batch mode, which incurs significant latency due to device-host memory transfers, thus resulting in the inflated observed runtimes (note, such memory transfer latency is negligible for small batch sizes, evidenced by SGD runtimes).  Additionally, in practice, large batch sizes in SGD have been observed to significantly decrease generalization performance [3,4], which is observed in the both the performance of (full batch) L-BFGS and for the proposed method (in Figure 4).  A fair comparison would be against L-BFGS designed for SGD from [2] with the same hyperparameters as kernel SGD, and AdaHessian should be compared to as well.

For the second point, several design choices for the method require further exploration.  In particular:
-" The last layer of the network can be regarded as the inference layer which has a similar decision function as general kernel machines. Thus, it is more natural to apply the update rule (4) only in the last fully connected layer, and the rest of the layers are updated using the original SGD." <- This is a hypothesis.  Did the authors attempt using Kernel SGD on all intermediate layers?  If so, could you please comment on the results of using the projection on all layers versus only using on the final layer?  If not, this is a large jump in logic without evidence to support it.
-A single RBF kernel is used.  However, an important point of exploration in this line of work would be how different kernel functions affect performance (even just a linear kernel).  Did the authors try other kernels?  And if so, could you please comment on this?
-In the convergence theorem proof, this result holds for any positive semi-definite matrix.  Thus, without further experiments, it isn't possible to assess the utility using a kernel matrix (which is unrelated to the Hessian of the actual DNN objective, see below) versus just random PSD projection matrices.

For the last point, note that while the authors claim that their set up conveniently sidesteps a number of difficulties encountered directly computing (or even estimating) the Hessian matrix in SGD, kernel SGD does not actually incorporate (or estimate) the DNN's Hessian.  The fact that the kernel matrix is the Hessian for kernel machine objectives does not equate to the very same kernel matrix providing Hessian-information for SGD with a completely different objective function.  The fact that the kernel matrix is called the Hessian matrix throughout the discussion of SGD is potentially misleading and may result in the reader to misunderstanding that the Hessian for the DNN objective is, indeed, being calculated in some form.
 
Other comments:
-"As for L-BFGS and ESGD which do not compute the Hessian matrix of
 neural networks explicitly, we recorded the memory for the components
 which are used to approximate the Hessian matrices in L-BFGS and
 ESGD." <- How exactly were these recorded in PyTorch?  This is an
 important, nontrivial detail and requires explanation.
 
"Therefore, the computation cost for Hessian matrix is rather small compared with the training of the
whole network." <-The described method is potentially burdensome in terms of both diskspace and loading the kernel matrix (and inverse) of each mini-batch into memory.  The kernel matrix (and inverse) for all minibatches is unlikely to fit in even large GPU device memories (e.g., 32 GB for V100) for modest problems and standard mini-batch sizes.  For instance, a mini-batch size of 512 requires a transfer of > 262k  parameters for a single step of SGD, repeated n/512 per epoch.  While only a mini-batch size of 64 was evaluated, what is the latency impact of this loading on speed as the mini-batch increases?

I have not seen primal/dual relationship for kernel machines explained
as it appears in Section 2.  Even w.r.t. the Keerthi paper referenced
(which deals with RBF SVMs), the explanation given is very different.
The notation and description of kernels is particularly confusing;
typically, one either solves primal problem to determine the w's or
the dual to determine the \alpha's... it is also extremely strange
that regularization occurs in the dual space (e.g., SVMs are typically
L1 or L2 normalized, which occurs in the primal objective space).
None the less, it is easy to see from the dual of an unregularized SVM
that the Hessian is thus the kernel matrix.  Note that, in the case of
a regularized SVM, this is not true (the regularization parameter
often crops up as a diagonal component).

References:
[1] Yao, Zhewei, et al. "ADAHESSIAN: An adaptive second order optimizer
for machine learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2006.00719 (2020).
[2] Bollapragada, Raghu, et al. "A progressive batching L-BFGS method for
machine learning." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR,
2018.
[3] Keskar, Nitish Shirish, et al. "On large-batch training for deep
learning: Generalization gap and sharp minima." arXiv preprint
arXiv:1609.04836 (2016).
[4] Goodfellow, Ian, Yoshua Bengio, and Aaron Courville. Deep
learning. MIT press, 2016.
content.summary_of_the_review: Very interesting idea and theoretical results.  However, relevant second-order optimizers are not compared to, there are issues with comparing against included benchmark competitors, relevant experiments justifying design decisions are not included, and the description of the method as incorporating second-order/Hessian information for the DNN objective function of interest is misleading.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.confidence: 2: You are willing to defend your assessment, but it is quite likely that you did not understand the central parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.

As ADAHESSIAN and multi-batch L-BFGS are very slow, the tests on larger data sets are in progress, but they have no hope to outperform Kernel SGD. *C2: Please comment on the results of using the projection on all layers versus only using on the final layer.*

R2: The results are shown in the following table. Using Kernel SGD in all the intermediate layers did not show a better generalization performance and convergence speed than just using Kernel SGD in the last layer. Applying Kernel SGD in the last layer is computation efficient and can perform more accurate prediction. Intuitively, integrating Kernel SGD to the final layer is more natural than to all the layers, because the last layer of the network can be regarded as the inference layer which has a similar decision function as general kernel machines. Therefore, in practice, we only adopt Kernel SGD in the last layer. We have added this discussion in Section 3.2.

| data set | train. accuracy (\%) | test accuracy (\%) | converg. Time (sec.) |
| - | -| -| -|
| mnist|96.78|94.74|2475.89|
| usps|91.10|85.55|36.19|

*C3: Please try other kernels rather than a single RBF kernel. It isn't possible to assess the utility using a kernel matrix without trying just random PSD projection matrices.*

R3:  Our results in the table below show that Kernel SGD with any kernel function can significantly outperform that with random PSD matrices. More specifically, for Kernel SGD with linear and polynomial kernel, the results are similar to Kernel SGD with RBF kernel. Moreover, we conducted experiments by replacing the projection matrix with a random PSD matrix. The training with a random PSD matrix shows a terrible performance on cifar10.

| data set | kernel type | train. accuracy (\%) | test accuracy (\%)| converg. time (sec.)|
|-|-|-|-|-|
|cifar10|rbf|100.00|83.30|475|

|cifar10|polynomial|100.00| 83.95 | 525.46|
|cifar10|random PSD|10.05|10.07| 267.60|
|mnist|rbf| 99.92| 97.94| 272|
|mnist|linear| 99.95 | 97.49 |181.27 |
|mnist|polynomial| 99.85 | 97.92| 185.34 |
|mnist|random PSD| 99.94 | 97.86 |100.17|

*C4: The kernel matrix is called the Hessian matrix throughout the discussion of SGD may result in the reader to misunderstanding that the Hessian for the DNN objective is being calculated in some form.*

R4: We have replaced the Hessian matrix with kernel matrix.

*C5: How exactly was the memory of Hessian in L-BFGS and ESGD recorded?*

R5: For L-BFGS, we recorded the memory consumption for storing the historical weights and gradients used in L-BFGS. In ESGD, we recorded the memory of the preconditioning matrix. We have added this explanation in the fourth paragraph of Section 4.2.

*C6: The described method is burdensome in terms of both diskspace and loading the kernel matrix. What is the latency impact of this loading as the mini-batch increases?*

R6: Kernel SGD is memory efficient (i.e., linear in the number of training data, cf. Section 3.2). As shown in Table 2 of the main text, the whole kernel matrix only needs 11.72 MB memory at most. Moreover, the size of kernel can be controlled by setting the mini-batch size. We have conducted experiments with increasing the mini-batch size as shown in Figure 4 in the main text, the efficiency of Kernel SGD is excellent. Please note that all of reported execution time in our manuscript has included the time of loading the kernel matrix.

*C7: The notation and description of kernel machines in Section 2 are confusing; Hessian is the kernel matrix for the dual of an unregularized SVM. In the case of a regularized SVM, this is not true.*

R7: Sorry for the confusion. We've improved Section 2.  Please note that the SVM representation we used is identical to the mainstream SVM libraries such as LibSVM and ThunderSVM. Due to the need to compute the second-order derivative, we need to use the intermediate step (i.e., Equation 2) from the primal to dual transformation. We'd like to stress that Equation 2 is not a regularization on the dual form, but just simply replacing $\boldsymbol{\omega}$ with $\sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j \phi(\boldsymbol{x}_j)$ in Equation 1.
